Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
I work hard at keeping busy with other things

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

vignette:
Amir was forty-eight, a fashion designer who had built his career on precision and control - clean lines, tailored fits, the exact weight of a fabric against the skin. Three years ago, he was at a premier fashion show held on the top floor of a downtown Manhattan high-rise when a faulty electrical panel ignited a fire that spread through the ventilation system. He remembered the heat first, sudden and thick, then the smell of burning synthetic fiber, a taste like ash that coated his tongue. He pushed through a crowd toward the emergency stairs, but the stairwell was already filling with smoke. He made it out, but for hours afterward he could not stop tasting that acrid sweetness, could not shake the sensation of heat on his arms. The official report called it a man-made disaster - negligent maintenance. For Amir, it became a fault line running through every ordinary moment.

In the months that followed, his memory of the event came back in disconnected fragments: the feel of a hot metal railing, a stranger's elbow in his ribs, the high-pitched alarm that seemed to come from inside his skull. The taste would surface without warning - at his drafting table, in the middle of a fitting - and when it did, the memory did not feel like something from the past. It felt as though he were back in that stairwell, the heat pressing in, the nausea rising in his throat. These intrusive moments were nearly impossible to predict. A specific temperature - the warmth of sunlight through a window, the heat of a hair dryer - could send his stomach turning. The same was true for sudden knots of nausea, which arrived with no apparent cause and pulled the scene into the present. After a memory fragment surfaced, even the simple act of stepping into a warm room felt like stepping into a trap, and he began to see potential triggers everywhere - in the glow of a streetlamp, in the hum of a radiator, in the faintest smell of something burning in a kitchen two blocks away.

Because the memory was so fragmented and so viscerally real, Amir found himself constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of danger - the placement of exits, the movement of people, the smell of smoke. He could not walk into a restaurant without identifying the nearest escape route, and he would sometimes leave a café if the only path to the door felt blocked. This vigilance drained his concentration; he lost track of conversations, missed details in fabric orders. When the taste of ash came back - and it always came back - it made him feel that danger was imminent, that the fire was still happening, which sharpened his scanning and escape planning even more. He became hyperaware of every door, every window, every shadow. On high-alert days, when his sense of threat was at its peak, the memories surfaced more readily - a flicker of light at the edge of his vision could bring the stairwell back whole, as if his nervous system were keeping the event on a short leash.

To manage the rising threat he felt, Amir adopted several strategies. He checked the locks on his apartment door three times before bed, then again before work, certain that a failure to secure his space would invite disaster. He kept himself ferociously busy - working late, taking on extra projects, filling every hour with sketches and client meetings - because stillness left room for the memory to surface. And when the taste of ash became overwhelming, when the heat seemed to prickle his skin, he hurt himself physically: he would press a thumbnail into his palm or run a razor across his forearm, just to release the pressure. These actions temporarily broke the spiral, but they also brought the memory back more vividly. After he checked the locks for a fourth time, he would smell the burning fabric again. After a long night at the drafting table, he would wake with the taste already in his mouth, the shame of what he had done to himself mixing with the dread. Each time he checked the locks or hurt himself to break the spiral, he was reinforcing the belief that the world was dangerous - the behaviours prevented him from ever learning that the threat had passed, so the sense of danger remained just as high as the day of the fire.

The cycle tightened over two years. Amir's marriage, already strained, could not survive the vigilance and the secrecy of his self-harm. His wife could not understand why he would not go to restaurants on the second floor, why he flinched when she turned on the oven. They divorced, and he moved into a ground-floor studio where he could see the street from every room. His occupation became both refuge and trap: the fitting rooms had no windows, and he would stand with his back to the wall, planning how to get out if the lights flickered. He lost two major accounts because his concentration faltered during presentations; a buyer noticed him staring at the ceiling vents. He told himself the hypervigilance kept him safe, but it also made him exhausted, brittle, and isolated.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was a morning in the showroom when a colleague lit a scented candle. The heat from the flame, the faint wisp of smoke - it triggered a memory so vivid that he felt the nausea rise and saw the stairwell door glow red. He rushed to the bathroom and cut his forearm with a broken plastic comb, then sat on the tile floor, shaking. He knew then that the strategies he had built were no longer containing the past; they were rebuilding it every day. He walked into a therapist's office the following week, afraid that talking about the fire would bring it back fully, but also afraid - perhaps more afraid - of what had started to feel inevitable.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that the memory itself causes or amplifies triggers; instead, triggers lead to memory.
The vignette does not show that the sense of threat causes the traumatic memory to surface; rather, memory leads to threat.
The vignette does not show that maladaptive strategies directly increase the sense of threat; they are used to reduce threat and indirectly lead to memory which then causes threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not show that the memory itself causes or amplifies triggers; instead, triggers lead to memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not show that the sense of threat causes the traumatic memory to surface; rather, memory leads to threat.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not show that maladaptive strategies directly increase the sense of threat; they are used to reduce threat and indirectly lead to memory which then causes threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
